lessons.content_md:
### Why this one is for you
Look at your own prompts from the last month. The `/clear` worktree bug shows up again and again:

- "The worktree session switching problem is not fixed..."
- "No, it still doesn't work. To reproduce, create a new session with /clear..."
- "I'm pretty sure I'm running the latest version, but the problem is still not fixed."

Four rounds on the same bug. Each time you checked the fix by hand, in the TUI, by typing `/clear` yourself. Hand checks are slow and they forget. A test does not forget. This lesson shows one prompt shape that makes the agent prove the bug is real *before* it is allowed to fix anything.

### The idea: red before green
A **regression test** is a small piece of code that fails when the bug is present and passes when the bug is gone. It sits in your repo forever and shouts if the bug comes back.

The trick is the order. Most people ask for a fix, then ask for a test. That test is written to match the fix, so it passes even if the fix is wrong.

Instead: make the agent write the test **first** and run it and show you it **failing**. A failing test is proof the agent understood the bug. Only then does it touch `agitrack/proxy/runner.py`.

Red first, then green.

### The prompt shape
Here is the shape. Notice it splits into two stops, and the agent must pause after the first.

```
Bug: after /clear in the native Claude backend, choosing a new
worktree keeps the session in the OLD worktree after restart.

Step 1: add a failing test to tests/test_proxy.py that reproduces
this. Run it. Paste the failure output. Do NOT touch any source
file yet. Stop and wait for me.

Step 2 (only after I say go): make the test pass. Do not change
the test to fit the code.
```

Three parts do the work: name the bug in reproduction steps, forbid source edits, and forbid editing the test later. That last line matters most. Without it the agent often "fixes" a stubborn test by loosening the test.

### Why the pause is worth it
Your digest says 20% of your turns run longer than 30 minutes. A long autonomous run that ends with "fixed!" is exactly where these four relapses hid.

The pause after step 1 costs you about thirty seconds and gives you the highest-value moment in the whole loop. You read the failure message. If it says something unrelated, or the test is asserting the wrong thing, you catch it *now* instead of after a 30 minute run plus another manual TUI session.

A failing test you have read is a contract. Both you and the agent now agree on what "fixed" means.

### Try this next time
In your very next aGiTrack session, pick any bug you are about to report and add these two lines to the end of your prompt:

```
First write a failing test that reproduces this, run it, and show
me the failure. Do not edit source yet. Then wait for my go-ahead.
When fixing, change the source, never the test.
```

You already have `tests/test_proxy.py` and `tests/FLOW_MATRIX.md` as homes for these. Since you type this shape often, it is a great candidate for your `AGENTS.md`: one standing rule instead of retyping it every bug.

exercise.hint: Start with 'Bug:' then 'To reproduce: 1... 2... 3... Expected... Actual...'. Then 'Step 1: ... Stop and wait.' Then 'Step 2 (after my go-ahead): ...'. The sentence people forget is the last one about never editing the test.

```
The worktree session switching problem is not fixed, and the
worktree mechanism is now basically broken when switching in
native agent. It should also work if someone types /clear and

```

This is the prompt shape that led to four relapses. Rewrite it as a test-first prompt. In your answer, include: (1) the bug stated as reproduction steps, (2) an instruction to write and run a failing test in `tests/test_proxy.py` with no source edits, (3) a stop-and-wait point, and (4) a rule that the fix must change source, not the test. Four to eight lines is plenty.

lessons.content_md:
### Why this one file keeps biting you
Look at your last month of prompts. Almost all of them say the same kind of thing: "the old session name became the new session's name", "it still stays in the same worktree", "restart shows the old name with the new session inside it".

Those are symptoms. Behind every one of them sits `agitrack/proxy/runner.py`, your most-changed file with 230 edits. It holds the small bit of state that says *which session am I in right now*.

When you describe a symptom, your agent has to guess which field is wrong. When you name the field, it goes straight there. That is the whole point of this lesson.

### The three fields, in plain words
Every session-name bug you reported is one of three values getting out of sync:

1. **session id** - the agent's own identifier for the conversation. Changes when you type `/clear`.
2. **worktree path** - the folder on disk this session commits into. A git worktree is just a second checkout of the same repo in its own directory.
3. **session name** - the human label you type when aGiTrack asks "name this session".

A healthy session has all three pointing at the same thing. Your bugs are all cases where one moved and the other two did not.

### Map your bugs onto the fields
Try matching your own reports:

```
"old session name becomes the name for the new session"
  -> session id changed, session name did not

"even if I choose to create a new worktree, it stays in the old one"
  -> session id changed, worktree path did not

"restart shows the old session's name with the new session inside it"
  -> worktree path was reloaded from disk, session name came from
     somewhere else, and they disagree
```

See the pattern? It is never "the name is broken". It is always "two of the three fields disagree, and here is which two".

### How to say it to your agent
Compare these two prompts for the same bug.

Symptom style, the one you have been typing:

> The worktree session switching problem is not fixed, and the worktree mechanism is now basically broken when switching in native agent.

Field style:

> In `agitrack/proxy/runner.py`, when the agent reports a new session id after `/clear`, the worktree path is not updated to match. Show me where the session id is read and where the worktree path is set, then explain why one updates and the other does not.

The second one names the file, the trigger, and the two fields that disagree. Your agent stops guessing and starts reading.

### Try this next time
Before your next bug report, ask yourself one question:

**Which two of session id, worktree path, session name disagree, and what event made them disagree?**

The event is usually one of: `/clear`, restart, quit before naming, or `--new-session`.

Then write the prompt as: *file + event + the two fields*. One sentence. That is it.

Bonus: your digest shows this same request keeps getting typed from scratch. Once you have a sentence that works, drop it in `AGENTS.md` as a short note like "session bugs live in runner.py; always name which of id / worktree / name is stale". Then you never have to rewrite it.

exercise.hint: The event is 'restart'. Ask yourself: on restart, where does each value get loaded from? If the worktree path is read back from disk but the session name comes from somewhere else, those are your two fields. Start your sentence with 'In agitrack/proxy/runner.py, on restart...'

lessons.content_md:
### You typed the same brief twice
Twice in this window you typed the long version of the same thing:

> Do a complete live repo test of aGiTrack, with all modes (including default, -b, -m, -b -m, --no-worktree). In interactive mode, use the TUI yourself. Cover all the modes and also...

And right after, you had to add a follow-up:

> Why are there only two scenarios for OpenCode parity? I think you need to run all the scenarios again for OpenCode backend once you are done with Claude backend.

That second message is the tell. The brief was long, but still incomplete. Typing it fresh each time means you drop something each time. Let's turn it into one short phrase that never forgets OpenCode.

### Write the brief down once
Your repo already has the right home for this: `tests/FLOW_MATRIX.md`, which you have touched 74 times. Make that file the single source of truth for what a full test run means.

```markdown
# Full live-repo matrix

Backends (BOTH, every time):
- claude
- opencode

Modes, for each backend:
- default
- -b
- -m
- -b -m
- --no-worktree

Interactive: drive the TUI yourself, do not stub it.
Done means: every backend x mode cell has a result line below.
```

Now the details live in a file instead of in your head.

### Make one phrase pull it in
Next, add a line to `AGENTS.md`, the file your agent reads before it starts. Something like:

```markdown
## Shortcut: "full matrix test"

When I say "run the full matrix", read tests/FLOW_MATRIX.md
and run every backend x mode cell in it. Both Claude and
OpenCode, no exceptions. Report a table of results.
```

That is the whole trick. "Skill" or "custom command" are just fancy names for this: a short phrase that expands into a long, complete instruction. Your ten-line brief becomes four words: **run the full matrix**.

### Let the file catch your corrections
Here is the part people skip. When the agent misses something, do not just correct it in chat. Fix the file too.

So when you found only two OpenCode scenarios, the fix is not only "run them all again". It is also one line added to `tests/FLOW_MATRIX.md`:

```markdown
Done means: every backend x mode cell has a result line below.
```

Now that gap can never come back. Each correction you land in the file is a correction you never type again. Your chat corrections are throwaway; your file is permanent.

### Try this next time
In your very next session, watch for the moment you start typing a long brief you have typed before. Stop, and do this instead:

1. Say: *"Write this brief into tests/FLOW_MATRIX.md as a checklist, then add a 'full matrix test' shortcut to AGENTS.md that points at it."*
2. Then run it with the short phrase.

Two minutes of setup, and every future run is four words instead of four lines. Bonus: the checklist is now something you can review and improve, which a chat message never was.

exercise.hint: Look at your own follow-up message about OpenCode parity. What word never appears in the shortcut above?


They then say "run the full matrix" and get back a neat table of five rows, all passing. But it is exactly the bug you already hit once.

In one or two sentences: what is missing, and write the extra line you would add to the shortcut to make sure it can never happen again.

Two minutes of setup, and every future run is four words instead of four lines. Bonus: the checklist is now something you can review and improve, which a chat message never was.

lessons.title: Bottle your full-matrix test request

suggestions.teaser: Write one sentence that states what must always be true, and watch the same fix survive restart, the yes path, and the no path on the first try.
suggestions.title: Turn a bug report into an invariant the agent must not break
suggestions.why: Your session-name and worktree fixes needed three to four rounds because 'also check the no path' and 'restart is what broke before' came only after the agent said done.

suggestions.teaser: You will be able to point at the exact line where a skill event is dropped, and say so in your next prompt instead of re-reporting the symptom.
suggestions.title: Follow one skill event from agent output to metadata file
suggestions.why: You have asked three separate times for skills to appear in metadata and it still silently does not; runner.py is your biggest rework file at 230 changes.

suggestions.teaser: Get the agent to print its scenario list first, so you catch missing coverage in thirty seconds rather than an hour later.
suggestions.title: Ask for the test matrix before the test run
suggestions.why: You had to ask 'why are there only two scenarios for OpenCode parity?' after a long full-matrix run had already finished.

suggestions.teaser: Next time CI goes red, you will know which workflow file and which pinned version line to name in your prompt.
suggestions.title: Read a red GitHub Action and find the pinned version yourself
suggestions.why: The Pages deploy failure was forwarded to the agent as a raw run link with a guess about Node.js rather than a located cause.
